lines: PRESIDENT:  Before Dr Abdulla joins, I would like to
express the tribunal's view on this case is that this
is a case where the issues of liability can be
separated from the issues of quantum.  And this is
indicated by the long adjournment we will now have
before hearing the quantum evidence in July.
So the tribunal would be greatly assisted if the
party could agree to submit their closing submission
on the issues of liability, for example, within the
14 days from now, while the evidence heard so far is
still fresh in the tribunal's mind.
Any further closing submission on quantum can be
made following the quantum evidence being heard on
15th July.  This is the tribunal's strong preference
at this stage.
Of course, you might go and discuss this and
receive instruction from your client, and I don't want
you now to answer this, but maybe before end of
today's hearing, we can get your reply.
Also, the tribunal direct that the closing
submission must be very focused on the agreed list of
issues, so that the submissions are drafted directly
in response to each of those issues.  Of course,
leaving out any issues of quantum to be addressed in
later submission following the quantum evidence.
Now we can, of course, agree later on on number of
pages, which is, my belief, the tribunal belief, maybe
shouldn't be more than 30 to 35 pages, but this is
something we can discuss at a later stage before end
of the hearing of today.
I hope I made myself very clear.  We need to
discuss this or get your feedback, not right now, of
course, but later on, at any time, at the break or
before end of the hearing of today.
MR WYGAS:  Of course, sir.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you very much for that.  I see now
Dr Abdulla is there.  Good morning.
DR TALEB:  Good morning.
PRESIDENT:  Yes.  Now we could proceed again with the
expert, who should be reminded again, he's still under
the oath.
Please proceed.
MR CHRISTIAN MERRETT (continued)
Cross-examination by MR BURKE (continued)
MR BURKE:  Thank you, sir.
Good morning, Mr Merrett.
A. Good morning.
Q. I suspect I don't need to take you to it, given your
presentation last night.  But you will recall that the
methodology that you've agreed for your delayed
analysis was the as-planned/as-built windows approach
as defined in the SCL Protocol, correct?
A. Yes.  That was mentioned in joint statement number 1.
Q. Yes.  And I think one of the differences, or at least
one of your views as to one of the differences between
you and Mr Falkenstern, is that you say, and I think
you said it a number of times last night, you say that
your analysis follows the SCL Protocol and
particularly the as-planned/as-built windows analysis,
whereas you believe Mr Falkenstern's does not.  Is
that right?
A. That's correct, yes.
Q. Could we look, please, at the SCL Protocol just to
orientate ourselves.
I'm sure everyone is very familiar with it.
It's at {K1}, page 40, please.
Mr Merrett, do you have a hard copy of your report
as well as the screen?
A. I have hard copies of everything, but not the SCL
Protocol.
Q. Okay.  It just makes it easier because I can take you
to parts of your report without necessarily having to
bring them up on the screen unless I need to for
everyone else.
A. Yes, okay.
Q. If we could just scroll, just down so we could see --
just the top of that.  Sorry, scroll.  So pull the
page down, exactly.  Just one more, please.  Yes, so
we can see -- that's fine, that's fine.  Thank you.
We can see the table 11.5.  We can see the various
types of delay analysis methodology that the protocol
identifies.  And we can see then at the top of {K1},
page 40, the as-planned versus as-built windows
analysis.  Do you see that?
A. That is correct.  Yes, I can see that.
Q. And that says, and do you agree, that it is an effect
and cause analysis.  Correct?
A. That is correct.  Yes.
Q. And that means you identify and quantify critical
delay first, and then you look to find out what caused
it, in that order?
A. That is correct, yes.
Q. And it requires you to identify -- so "it" being the
as-planned/as-built windows analysis requires you to
identify the critical path contemporaneously?
A. It does.
Q. And then to determine the impact or to determine the
causes of critical delay retrospectively.  Is that
correct?
A. Yes.  That's correct.
Q. If we then look to 11.6(d), which is on page {K1-41},
I think it's just two pages down, we see, 11.6, there
is the descriptions in narrative form of the various
forms of analysis.
If we then go to the bottom -- sorry.  Scroll
down, please, to 41.  Yes.  Bottom of page 41.  And
could we have the bottom of page 41 and the top of
page 42 because that -- yeah, that's perfect.
This paragraph, which is 11.6(d) of the protocol,
defines or describes the as-planned versus as-built
windows analysis; is that right?
A. That is correct, yes.
Q. And this is what you agreed with Mr Falkenstern's
predecessor was the appropriate form of analysis in
this case, correct?
A. That's correct.  Yes.
Q. And if we look at how that is described, and I'll
quote from the protocol:
"The as-planned versus as-built windows analysis
method is the second of the 'windows' analysis
methods.  As distinct from a time slice analysis, it
is less reliant on programming software and usually
applied when there is concern over the validity or
reasonableness of the baseline programme and/or the
contemporaneously updated programmes and/or where
there are too few contemporaneously updated
programmes..."
It then goes on to explain that the way this is
done is by breaking down the duration of the works
into windows.  They are framed with reference to
programmes, updates, milestones, or significant
events.
And then what you as an analyst need to do is to
determine:
"... the contemporaneous or actual critical path
in each window by a common-sense and practical
analysis of the available facts.  As this task does
not substantially rely on programming software, it is
important that the analyst sets out the rationale and
reasoning by which criticality has been determined."
So that's the first step in the analysis, is how
you determine the as-built critical path.  Is that
right?
A. That's what it says, yes.
Q. Is that what you have done?
A. It is.  My -- obviously, my starting point was the
programmes, the programme updates.
Q. Well, let's look at your rationale and reasoning.
You agree, because this is what you say you've
done, that it is important to set out your rationale
and reasoning in your report so it can be understood
by the tribunal?
A. Sorry, was that a question?
Q. It was a question for you.
You agree, because you say that you've done this,
that it's important to set out your rationale and
reasoning by which criticality has been determined in
your report?
A. Yes, I agree.
Q. Could we then go, please, to {D2.2-76}.
This is your first report, and I'd like that on
the screen so that everyone can see it.  And here is
where you describe how you determine the as-built
critical path.  Is that right?
A. That is correct.
Sorry, the reference is {D2.2-76}.
Q. It's internal page -- well, it's PDF page 67.  It's
internal page 53, if you recall.
A. Yeah, I have the paginated versions.  That's fine.
Q. And this is where you describe how you determined
criticality, and what you say here, and this is 8.2.1,
is that you've:
"... used [your client's] programme updates
contained in [monthly progress reports] from
February 2023 to October 2023 to establish the
as-built critical path through the remaining works of
the Project after Addendum 4."
And then you go on to say that you've done that
by -- so you've established -- this is 8.2.2:
"I have established the as-built critical path
changes by an observational review of the longest
critical paths shown in the Respondent's monthly
programme updates."
Do you see that?
A. I do.
Q. When you say "an observational review of the longest
critical paths shown in the Respondent's monthly
programme updates", you mean that you've looked at
what the baseline programme you've chosen and the
various monthly progress updates say the critical path
is, and you have adopted that as your critical path;
correct?
A. Well, I look at the programme updates as the works are
progressed through addendum 4 and look at the point of
the data date what the status of the works were and
the works back behind that, and also what is critical,
shown on the data date.
Q. Yes.  So in order to determine what is critical, you
have taken what the programme and the programme update
says is critical, haven't you?
A. I've looked at the actual dates, the as-built dates,
as well as what is critical on the status date.
That's correct.
Q. Yes.  So you have relied heavily on the programming
software, the programme and the programming software
in order to determine your critical path, haven't you?
A. I wouldn't say -- I wouldn't agree I relied "heavily",
I think the emphasis "heavily" is incorrect, or it's
not a proper representation.  It's a starting point.
Q. Well, if we look at -- this is your, how you describe
your as-built critical path, how you describe how
you've determined the as-built critical path.
According to this description, it is both the
starting point and the end point, isn't it?  You don't
say anything else about how you've done it?
A. The critical path is determined by -- criticality only
really occurs on a measured activity when it fails to
meet its completion date --
Q. We'll get to that.
A. Could I just, if it's possible to just finish
a second.
So it needs to -- a lot of people tend to monitor
the progress of the activity through its duration.
I think only really true critical delay, and I believe
this states this in the SCL Protocol, can only be
established from when the late dates have been
breached, and then you know that the actual activity
has not finished at its very latest date and
therefore, from that point onwards, there's no more
float and it starts to incur critical delay.
The only real ideal method for a job of this
complexity, I think it needs to be only really started
at from the programme.  That's a good starting point.
Q. Well, I would suggest to you, Mr Merrett -- and if
there is a part of your report where you explain where
you've done anything other than use the critical path
that is shown to you by the programmes and the
programming software, I'm sure you'll be taken to it
in re-examination.
But you have used your client's programmes and
programme updates in order to determine your critical
path, haven't you?
A. I have, and they were issued, as I understand it, up
to Bapco, and they were part of a lengthy document.
Q. Do you accept that if you're going to rely on a
programme and programme updates, you need to make sure
that a number of things are right in those programmes?
And I'll walk through what those are.
First of all, do you agree that you need to make
sure that the logic of the programme makes sense, that
it's appropriate?
A. There's a bit of a misconception with regards to the
logic, and let me explain, is that as you update a
programme -- and I don't want to refer back to the
software because that's not necessarily going to be
very helpful.
But when you update a programme on an interim
basis or on a regular basis, the planner or the site
team therefore identify when things are actually
completed or the actual progress of those.
The baseline programme and its logic on the
updates is normally overridden.  So irrespective of
what logic is in the programme, that is overridden by
the actual updates that are implemented by the planner
or the construction team updating the programme.
Q. Yes.  So the product of the exercise that you've
done -- let me tell you what I suggest to you are the
three main things, three main elements that go into
that that I suggest you have to verify.
The first of them is the programme logic.
The second of them is the progress data that's
updated on each monthly progress cycle.
And the third is the remaining durations shown in
the programme.
Do you agree that they are three important things
that influence the critical path that is demonstrated
by the programmes and the programme updates?
A. I think the programme logic that you refer to is
probably getting slightly conflated with the planned
logic.
We know that the actual -- the dates, the
milestone dates, and the sequence of activities was
issued on a programme and updated on that programme.
And the updates, what I do know have occurred,
during the, I think it's six or seven programme
updates that I've been given access to, I believe them
to be correct.
Q. And you believe them to be correct because you have
verified them to be correct?
A. I look at the activities that are on the critical path
to see that those dates are there or pretty much
correct, in accordance with the contemporaneous
information, the records.
Q. Let's take an example.  If the progress data that's
used to generate a particular monthly programme
update, a monthly progress update, if that's wrong, if
there's a mistake in that, that can lead to the
programme suggesting the critical path is in the wrong
place, can't it?
A. Yes, it can.  And similarly, that also flips the other
way in regards to the, obviously that relates to
issues such as manpower that relates to the programme
and the progress updates that I believe Mr Falkenstern
has relied upon.
So equally, if there is an error, such as you
refer to, then that would also have the same or
similar effect to the data that Mr Falkenstern has
relied upon.
Q. Mr Merrett, what I'm suggesting -- I'm not for the
moment seeking to compare you and Mr Falkenstern.  I'm
suggesting that what you have done, what you need to
do, in order to rely on the programmes in the way that
you have, is to verify, to do some exercise of
verification, that the progress data that is being
input into each progress cycle is accurate.  Do you
agree with me?
A. Well, I don't agree with you in that -- let me explain
why I don't agree with you fully.
What we do know is neither myself or
Mr Falkenstern were on the job at the time.
So there is, as you've seen, there's monthly
reports, extensive monthly reports, and weekly
reports.  In fact, I will admit that there's a lot of
reporting on the job.
Now, these reports have been issued to the other
parties -- to the claimant.  And at that point,
I haven't seen anywhere where anybody's raised an
actual issue with a challenge or believe the programme
updates to be incorrect.
Now, there is a degree -- having been on
construction sites most of my life, there is -- we
don't have access to -- we don't have access to every
single --
PRESIDENT:  Sorry to interrupt.
Maybe, Dr Abdulla, I just remind you to be muted
maybe.
DR TALEB:  Oh, thank you very much.  Thank you.
I appreciate.
PRESIDENT:  Thank you.
Sorry.
A. Sorry.  I'll continue.  Sorry.
So we don't have access to every granular detail
of the progress updates.
Now, we don't have access to the handbooks or the
notepads that the planners had to make his notes on to
verify his updates.  We don't necessarily have access
to every single handover sheet.  What we have to do is
place a certain degree of reliance initially on the
validity of the updates.
And if we do, within reason, see anything that
might flag an inconsistency, then we deal with it.
And we also look at other documents outside the
programme to verify that and take a judgment on it.
MR BURKE:  So have you -- and if you have, perhaps you
could let me know where in your report you say that
you've done this or you explain the process that
you've done.
Have you sought to verify the progress data that's
in each monthly progress report with reference to the
rest of the as-built data, whether that's the other
progress data, whether that's weekly meeting minutes,
whether that's correspondence, whether that's the
whole as-built project record that you have.  Have you
done that verification exercise?
A. I have where necessary, yes, on certain occasions, if
I think there's something that was questionable.
We also rely on, as you've seen in the windows
that we've -- the analysis of the window periods, we
have seen documents that relate to causes of delay and
we try to the best that we possibly can align those.
We're not able to actually identify specific,
specific documents on a specific day.  On certain
things you can.  But there are a whole host of
documents in regards to records of late handovers in
trenches in regards to FEIs that have been issued, and
they cover a certain period.  But to nail it down to
an exact day, it's very difficult to do that in this
exercise.  There's a whole lot of data, as
Mr Falkenstern has quite rightly pointed out in his
cross-examination yesterday.
Q. Where -- if you could just help me, I'm sure you know
your reports very well.  Where do you explain the
context of the first step of your analysis?  I'm not
talking about identifying causes of critical delay.
I'm talking about determining the critical path.
Where do you identify -- and if you don't know
offhand, we can give you the time over the break to
look at it -- the exercise of verification you've done
to make sure that the monthly progress updates you've
used accurately reflect the rest of the as-built data?
A. Well, the verification process, as I've said before,
we rely on the programme updates because we have no --
this has been issued in the witness statements of
Mr Laoagan, as I understand.  And those native files
that he relies upon, that he is giving evidence on,
I give him some credibility and trust in his
professionalism as to give those updates some
accuracy.
If I believe, if I see on further examination that
those dates are questioned, then I will examine that.
You've got to bear in mind there are thousands of
activities in this programme.  It is not reasonable or
nor proportionate to check every single activity.  And
that's not what the expert is necessarily engaged to
do is to check every single activity.
Q. Mr Merrett, I'm simply trying to help the tribunal to
understand what you've done and what you haven't done.
If the answer is, "I have used the programme
updates because I assumed them to be accurate, and
I assumed them to be accurate because there was a
witness statement that said they were there", then
that's your evidence.  There's nothing more to it than
that.
A. No, no.  That's incorrect.  That's a
mischaracterisation of what I've said.
We start at the programmes and if we deem it
appropriate, then I will examine documents outside the
programme updates themselves, only if I see if it's
required.
Q. Is there anything -- I'm sorry.
A. If -- I'm sorry, could I -- yeah.
If I believe them -- if I have a suspicion or an
understanding or a concern that something might be
inaccurate, and also bearing in mind that we have had,
we've looked at extensive information, not in the same
manner that Mr Falkenstern has, because his approach
is completely different from mine, where he relies on
manpower.  But nevertheless, I've relied on programme
updates, which are the conventional way.
It doesn't say, it it doesn't say in the SCL
Protocol that you must take verification checks of all
the documents.
Q. Again, Mr Merrett, I'm trying to understand for the
tribunal's benefit what you've done and haven't done.
Presumably you're comfortable with what you have
done.  Are you able to now point to anywhere in your
report where you explain that there was an issue or an
anomaly that you've noticed in the as-built data, and
you've then identified that and then gone back and
corrected the programme in order to remove that
anomaly?
Is there an example of an explanation I can see in
your report where you explain that process that you've
just described?
A. I haven't carried out any physical changes to the
programme or updated or changed any of the dates of
the programme, no.
Q. All right.
So we've talked about logic.  We've talked about
progress data.
The other, what I would suggest to you, important
thing that you need to make sure makes sense is the
remaining durations and sequences in the programme.
Do you agree with that?
A. No, I don't.  The reason being is that this is a
contemporaneous analysis.  This is where, in my
opinion, of course, I believe -- and I have to make
reference to Mr Falkenstern to put this into context.
It appears that Mr Falkenstern relies heavily, or
just relies upon, whatever the remaining -- and he
mentioned it in his, I think it was his
cross-examination or presentation, I can't recall
which one, but he referred to remaining duration.
Again, I use the word "conflated".  There's a
misunderstanding in regards to remaining duration and
float, and our whole job, our whole job, if you're
trying to boil it down into a short explanation, is to
see what is critical.
Now, remaining durations and remaining man hours
or quantities do not by themselves establish
criticality.  They don't have any relevance to them.
What you're doing is you are tracking the progress
at the time and what you see at the time
contemporaneously to be the delay.
So, looking to the right -- as I would coin the
phrase, looking to the right-hand side of the data
date is a forecast.  Simply a forecast.  And tomorrow
is another day.
What we're looking at is we're looking at after
the fact -- that's what we're here for -- after the
works have been constructed, or not, as the case may
be.
Q. So your view is that it is no part of a
contemporaneous critical path assessment to make sure
that future sequences and durations for the works are
reasonable, realistic, and achievable.
You don't think that's a required element of a
contemporaneous critical path analysis that uses
programming and programming software?
A. No, I never said that.
What I'm -- you don't ignore it completely.
You're aware of it because you can't not be -- when a
programme is updated, there is a status of all the
activities that are not started, are either ongoing or
completed.
And you also -- because part of the function of
the programme is it tells you what is remaining of the
activity, but it also tells you what is remaining of
the float, or if any float has to be consumed.
So no, you can't ignore that.  What you must do is
take that in consideration, but what we're looking at
is on the data date, and then we look back
retrospectively.
That is the whole part of the process.  This is
what you took me to in the SCL Protocol.
Q. Just let me try one more time, Mr Merrett, because
I think you said "no", and then the answer you gave
was more consistent with an answer of "yes".
Is it your opinion that a contemporaneous critical
path assessment, such as is required by the
as-planned/as-built analysis, does not require the
analyst to verify that the future sequences and
durations in the programme are reasonable, realistic
and achievable.  Do you think that's a required
element of your analysis?
A. We take cognisance of it, but we do not rely on it for
the analysis of our delay.
Q. Even though your critical path is primarily generated
by the programme and the programming software, yes?
A. It's calculated on what is remaining in the durations
and the float.  But the float, which is also being
consumed, which is partly prospective, correct.
That's why I say you must take cognisance of it.
But what you do realise is that the programming
software will tell you or alert you when issues or
activities become critical.
Q. And the float -- and I'm trying very hard to avoid
getting into an esoteric discussion about float,
Mr Merrett.
But float is a product of the programming logic
and the progress data and the future sequences, isn't
it?  So that's what generates the float in the
programme?
A. That's what generates the remaining float and, yes,
the float.  Correct.
Q. Yeah.  And so in order to take proper attention of the
float, you do need to make sure that the programming
logic is appropriate, the progress data is
appropriate, and the remaining durations and sequences
are realistic, reasonable and achievable; yes?
A. Well, I think the fact that we're experts and we've
all been on construction sites -- or hopefully we
have -- allows us to apply, as the SCL Protocol says,
common sense.
So, yes.  So you wouldn't just take a programme
and, to probably refer you back to your previous
questions, you wouldn't rely on the programme alone.
I know things, things, activities, very well on
site, and I can tell you now there are a sequence in
which things should be carried out, a very strict
sequence, especially when -- I mean, as Mr Falkenstern
refers to in his evidence the other day, is that
essentially they could work anywhere.
Well, what we're saying now, the discussion we're
having now is we're acknowledging the fact that the
programme has a logical, and -- I will use the word
very lightly -- constrained or dictated sequence,
which is logic.  And out of that logic naturally comes
float.
Q. Yes.  And it is that product of the programme that
you've used for your critical path, your as-built
critical path.  Correct?
A. That is correct, yes.
Q. If we look, please -- we talked a little bit about, or
you talked a little bit about anomalies and about
potential correction of anomalies.
I think you know Mr Falkenstern has raised some
specific issues in his reports around aspects of your
critical path.  Perhaps we could look at some of them
now.
Could we look, please, at {D2.2-139}.  It should
be your chart for lot 5, I think.  Is that right?
A. It is lot 5, correct.  Yes.  Figure 37.
Q. Yes, exactly.  Figure 37.  Page {D2.2-139}.  Yes.
Just so I am clear that I understand what I'm
looking at, this, in green, is your baseline
programme?
I'm going to neutrally call it your baseline
programme for now.  We will talk about it.
A. Yes.
Q. Is that right?
A. That is for this discussion.  Yeah, that's correct.
Q. We will talk about the baseline programme, so neither
of us feel constrained to overly dance on the head of
a pin around references to baseline programmes in this
context.
The green is the as-planned from your baseline
programme.  The blue bars is your critical path taken
from the baseline programme and the progress updates,
correct?
A. No, not necessarily.  You'll see in the legend here
it's the as-built activity.  So that's the actual
recorded, the actual dates that have been updated --
are basically an outcome of the programme updates.
Q. Apologies, yeah.  Sorry.  So the blue is effectively
the progress data elements of these activities.  And
the red is the critical path, your critical path
generated by that.  Correct?
A. That is correct, yes.
Q. If we look at unit -- so between 1st April 2023 and
25th July 2023, you can see the red bar, kind of a
third of the way down the page?  That is the subgrade
concrete paving works at unit 56.  Do you see that?
A. That's correct, yes, yes.
Sorry.  Yes, 933 you mean.
Q. It's the second green bar down and if you follow it
along, you get to the first red bar, which has
17 days.
A. Yes, that's correct.  Sorry.  Yes.  Yeah.
Q. So 17 days.  And your opinion is that there were
17 days of critical delay to that activity, so the
subgrade concrete paving works at unit 56, between
I think it is 9th July and 25th July.  Is that right?
A. That's correct, yes.
Q. Now, I think you know, because it's in
Mr Falkenstern's second report, that Mr Falkenstern
has said that the concrete paving work at unit 56, so
this specific activity, had all been finished by
23rd June.  Are you aware of that?
A. Not specifically, but I'll indulge what you're saying.
Q. Okay.  If he is right, if the concrete paving works at
unit 23 had been completed by 23rd June, so before the
start of -- when you say critical delay starts to
accrue, would you accept that your critical path would
be wrong?
A. I would if I --
Q. Because it would be through an activity that had been
finished weeks before?
A. I would if I thought Mr Falkenstern's assessment was
correct.  But I don't, because, as I've said before,
he relies on pretty much prospective remaining work
and man hours.  And he, as I understand it, develops
a threshold, which I don't fully understand his
methodology, but he has a threshold of a 2 per cent
threshold, which I believe was in cross-examination
yesterday, which I don't fully understand.
And if I don't understand something, then I can't
necessarily conclusively agree that he is right, that
he's right and I'm actually wrong.
What I'm referring to, with a certain amount of
faith and a certain amount of scrutiny of the
information, is that based on the programme updates --
and I do believe there are some differences in
progress updates, as we've seen yesterday -- is that
there is 17 days' critical delay, ie the activity, the
planned activity that consumed its float on the
progress records that are updated and issued to the
claimant, was now, based on that information, showing
17 days' delay on that programme assessment.
Q. Mr Merrett, what I'm asking you, it's a much more
straightforward question around the facts rather than
any form of analysis.
My suggestion to you is that the subgrade concrete
paving works at unit 56 had in fact been finished by
23rd June.  There were no more works remaining of that
activity after 23rd June.
And I'm suggesting to you that if that's right as
a fact, then that would make you -- force you to
rethink your critical path during this period, yes?
A. If it was, but I don't believe it is.
